newsitem.title: GERMANY: Metro profits up, but outlook gloomy.
newsitem.headline: Metro profits up, but outlook gloomy.

text.p: Newly-merged German retailer Metro AG announced first half results on Thursday which showed a gain in profits on flat sales, but some analysts were disappointed by a downgrade in the company's full year profit forecast.

Group operating profits after goodwill writedowns rose to 181 million marks ($119 million) from 48 million marks. But profits were still tiny in comparison to group turnover of 29.1 billion marks, just below 29.2 billion marks in the same period of 1995.
The company said it expected a full-year pre-tax profit of between 1.0 and 1.1 billion marks, assuming no unexpected events and pre-Christmas business in line with last year.
But that was down from a forecast of 1.12 billion marks published ahead of Metro's first listing in July.
"It's not exactly a strong result," said retail analyst Michael Wand of Paribas in Frankfurt, adding that the outlook amounted to a "downgrade through the back door."

Analysts said Metro would struggle to quadruple profits in the traditionally stronger second half from normal operations, but may be able to top up the figure lower down in the profit and loss account.
"The numbers are a bit disappointing and I will be revising my forecast down," Michael Bahlmann of MM Warburg told Reuters.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett said in a note, however, that the half year figures should be viewed neutrally and this year's profit target was achievable.

Metro shares have barely moved since their first listing in July after the group fused with ASKO Deutsche Kaufhaus AG, Deutsche SB-Kauf AG and Kaufhof Holding AG to become one of Germany's leading retail empires.

The shares traded up in a record-setting market on the results which, although uninspiring, spared investors any unpleasant surprises. The stock was up 4.40 marks to 140.40 marks at 1045 GMT, still around its launch price.

ABN AMRO's team said it was keeping its buy recommendation on the stock, with a six-month target of 190 marks, while Paribas' Wand said investors should hold Metro shares as they were unlikely to outperform the DAX index.
Wand said he was trimming his earnings per share forecast for 1996 to seven marks, and Warburg's Bahlmann said he would probably do so as well.

A spokesman for Swiss-controlled Metro said profit margins were improving following the merger, but that the overall business was being hit by poor demand. Metro recently revised down its 1996 full-year sales forecast by three billion marks to 62 billion marks.
"The consumer climate...did not significantly improve in July and August or in the first weeks of September," Metro said in a statement.
"Uncertainty over Germany's economic future as a place to do business in general and job fears mark consumer attitudes," Metro said, adding there was no prospect of a pickup next year.

Germany's economy is suffering from near-record post-war unemployment of over 10 percent but is starting to emerge from a winter trough. Metro said it doubted economic forecasters who predict a revival in the all-important Christmas season.

First half operating profits from Metro's 14 divisions came in at 273 million marks, up from 89 million, with strong gains in media, mail order and the SB store chain. Those gains were partly erased by an increase in holding operations costs.
The company invested 620 million marks in the first half, and expanded sales area by 1.9 percent to 7.3 million square metres. Full-time staff were reduced by 4.1 percent to 130,495.
